subtype: Approach: wait for it to pass through sleeping and scrolling [Pitfall]
passage:
For weeks my whole routine was: sleep till noon, scroll, lie there, repeat. I told myself it was just a phase and that if I waited long enough I'd wake up feeling normal. Some days I skipped meals because getting up felt like too much work.

The strange part is that the phone kept my hands busy while my mind went quieter and quieter. The bed got heavier, the curtains stayed closed, and messages piled up. Nobody noticed for about a month because I answered with a thumbs-up and said I was busy.

When Vasudha came over and found me still in yesterday's clothes at four in the afternoon, she sat on the floor and asked me one question: 'What's been going on?' That was the first time I said it out loud. Jatin

qa.q: What time was it when Vasudha found Jatin in yesterday's clothes?
qa.a: It was four in the afternoon.

qa.q: What might Jatin have been feeling while telling everyone 'I'm busy' from bed?
qa.a: Jatin was probably low and withdrawn, wanting the mood to lift by itself and not wanting to worry anyone.

qa.q: What could Jatin have tried in the first week instead of waiting, and why?
qa.a: Jatin could have told someone or asked a counsellor for help, because sleep and scrolling did nothing to change the low mood and only delayed support.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have felt when she saw Jatin that afternoon?
qa.a: Vasudha was probably worried and gentle, choosing to sit on the floor and ask an open question instead of lecturing.

grounding: A person sleeps late, scrolls and stays in bed hoping the mood lifts alone, and weeks pass before anyone notices.

subtype: Approach: wait for it to pass through sleeping and scrolling [Pitfall]
passage:
Warden's note, 2 December. Pallavi, girls' hostel, second floor.
The mess staff told me that Farida, B.Com final year, hasn't come for breakfast or lunch in about three weeks. The attendance office says she has missed most lectures since early November. Nobody raised it earlier; her roommate thought she was studying online.
I knocked at noon today. The curtains were closed and she was in bed with her phone. She said she'd been sleeping at four or five and waking in the afternoon, scrolling most of the time in between. 'I thought if I rested enough, I'd feel normal again,' she said. 'But it just stays the same.'
When I asked gently, she said she has had no thoughts of harming herself, but she does feel 'far away from everything'.
I sat with her while she called her mother, and walked her to the counselling centre this afternoon; she has a session tomorrow at ten. I will check on her again tonight and tomorrow morning.

qa.q: How long has Farida missed breakfast and lunch?
What does Farida mean by feeling 'far away from everything'?
qa.a: She feels detached and low, as if the days are passing without her, even after all the rest.

qa.q: What could have helped Farida earlier than three weeks in?
qa.a: A small daily routine with a fixed waking time and meals, and telling someone early, since rest and scrolling alone kept her stuck.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Pallavi, the warden who wrote the note?
qa.a: Pallavi realises weeks passed unnoticed and responds the same day with a call home, a counselling slot and check-ins.

grounding: Shows a student sleeping late, scrolling and staying in bed hoping the mood lifts, until weeks pass before anyone notices.

subtype: Approach: wait for it to pass through sleeping and scrolling [Pitfall]
passage:
Thursday, 4:10 p.m. Jahnavi's diary.
Just woke up. Again. Went to sleep around five, after scrolling short videos until the sky went grey. I keep thinking tomorrow I'll wake up feeling like myself, and then tomorrow is exactly this.
It's been maybe four weeks. I've stopped going to Sunday dance practice. I've stopped cooking. I told myself I just need rest, and rest means bed and phone. But I'm more tired now than when I started resting.
Nobody's noticed, which is sort of the point and sort of the worst part.
Update, 9 p.m. Shreya came to return my charger and saw the room. She didn't say anything about the mess. She sat on the bed and said, 'You haven't been at practice in a month. What's going on?' I said 'nothing' and then cried for twenty minutes. She stayed. We looked up the student counselling line together and booked tomorrow's first slot, and she's coming with me.

qa.q: What time did Jahnavi go to sleep?
What does 'more tired now than when I started resting' reveal?
qa.a: Jahnavi feels drained and discouraged, seeing that the sleeping and scrolling have not helped at all.

qa.q: What could Jahnavi try alongside counselling?
qa.a: A set waking time and one small activity each day, like going back to dance practice, instead of waiting in bed for the mood to lift.

qa.q: What might Shreya be feeling as she sits on the bed?
qa.a: Worried and caring, having noticed the missed practices, and glad to have come in person.

grounding: Shows a young person sleeping late and scrolling in bed for weeks hoping the mood lifts, until a friend finally notices.
